option1: Create MediaAdapter implements MediaPlayer, holding an AdvancedMediaPlayer field, and have its play(filename) internally decide whether to call playVlc() or playMp4() based on file type
option2: Create a static utility method MediaUtils.convert(AdvancedMediaPlayer p) that returns a String
option3: Modify AdvancedMediaPlayer directly to implement MediaPlayer
option4: Make Mp3Player extend AdvancedMediaPlayer so it inherits playVlc()/playMp4()
correctOptionExplanation: The adapter satisfies the interface your app expects (MediaPlayer) while wrapping the incompatible third-party class and translating the call internally.

questionText: In the MediaAdapter from the previous question, why must AdvancedMediaPlayer be held as a field (composition) rather than MediaAdapter extends AdvancedMediaPlayer (inheritance)?
option1: There's no real reason — both approaches are functionally identical in every case
option2: Java doesn't allow multiple inheritance of classes, and MediaAdapter already needs to implements MediaPlayer while also gaining AdvancedMediaPlayer's behavior — composition avoids ever needing to extend two classes at once, and also works even if AdvancedMediaPlayer were final
option3: Because interfaces cannot be implemented by any class that also extends something
option4: Because AdvancedMediaPlayer has private fields, inheritance is impossible in any language
correctOptionExplanation: Composition sidesteps Java's single-inheritance limit entirely, which is why it's the default choice for adapters.

option2: This is wrong — TemperatureSensor should be a concrete class, not an interface, for adapters to work
option3: This is correct — it implements the expected interface, wraps the incompatible class, and translates the value inside the overridden method
option4: This is wrong — getCelsius() should just call sensor.getFahrenheit() directly without conversion
correctOptionExplanation: This is a textbook-correct adapter: satisfies the target interface, wraps the incompatible object, converts the value inline.

questionText: The "square peg in a round hole" teaching example: you have RoundHole.fits(RoundPeg peg) and want to fit a SquarePeg (which only has getWidth()) into it without modifying RoundHole or SquarePeg. What must the adapter provide to satisfy RoundHole.fits(RoundPeg peg)'s method signature?
option1: A method on SquarePeg itself called asRoundPeg()
option2: Change RoundHole.fits() to accept Object instead of RoundPeg
option3: There's no way to adapt a square peg to a round hole — the shapes are fundamentally incompatible
option4: A class like SquarePegAdapter extends RoundPeg (or implements the same type RoundHole.fits expects) that wraps a SquarePeg and computes an equivalent radius from its width inside an overridden method
correctOptionExplanation: The adapter must be shaped exactly like what fits() expects (a RoundPeg), computing an equivalent value from the square peg's own data.

option2: Incorrect — StripeAdapter should extend StripeClient so no wrapping is needed
option3: Incorrect — the adapter shouldn't do any unit conversion; that logic belongs inside StripeClient, which you'd need to modify
option4: Incorrect — pay() should call stripeClient.charge() with the dollar amount unconverted
correctOptionExplanation: Unit translation (dollars to cents) is exactly the kind of work an adapter is meant to absorb, keeping the mismatch invisible to callers.

questionText: Suppose two teams each write an adapter for the same StripeClient, but one team's adapter also logs the transaction before calling stripeClient.charge(), and the other team's doesn't. Is this still a valid Adapter pattern usage?
option1: No — adding logging makes it a Decorator instead of an Adapter
option2: Yes — Adapter only requires the wrapper to satisfy the target interface and internally use the incompatible class; anything else the adapter's overridden method does (logging, retries, etc.) is an implementation detail, not a violation of the pattern
option3: Yes, but only if the logging happens inside StripeClient itself instead
option4: No — Adapter classes must contain nothing but a single delegating call with zero extra logic
correctOptionExplanation: Adapter's requirement is about satisfying the target interface while bridging an incompatible class — extra logic inside that bridge doesn't disqualify it.

questionText: You maintain an IShipping interface with double calculateCost(double weightKg, String destination). A newly-acquired vendor's shipping API instead exposes ShippingQuote getQuote(ShippingRequest request), where ShippingRequest is a whole separate class you'd need to construct. What's the correct adapter shape?
option1: Have every caller of IShipping construct a ShippingRequest themselves before calling calculateCost()
option2: Skip the adapter and have IShipping extend the vendor's client class directly
option3: VendorShippingAdapter implements IShipping, wrapping the vendor's client object; inside calculateCost(), it constructs a ShippingRequest from the given parameters, calls the vendor's getQuote(), and extracts/returns the numeric cost from the resulting ShippingQuote
option4: Change IShipping.calculateCost()'s signature to accept a ShippingRequest directly, so no translation is needed
correctOptionExplanation: The adapter absorbs the complexity of constructing the vendor-specific request object and unpacking its response, keeping the target interface simple.

questionText: Why is it better for VendorShippingAdapter to construct the ShippingRequest object internally, rather than changing IShipping.calculateCost() to accept a ShippingRequest parameter directly?
option1: ShippingRequest cannot be constructed inside another class in Java
option2: It's not actually better — changing the interface signature is the correct approach
option3: IShipping.calculateCost() can only accept primitive types by language restriction
option4: Changing IShipping's signature would force every existing caller across the whole codebase to know about and construct vendor-specific ShippingRequest objects, defeating the purpose of having a stable target interface that hides vendor-specific details
correctOptionExplanation: Keeping the target interface stable and vendor-agnostic is the whole reason to introduce an adapter in the first place.

option1: This is a valid adapter — it satisfies every method Duck requires, mapping quack() to gobble() and approximating fly() via repeated short flights, without modifying Turkey
option2: Invalid — TurkeyAdapter must extend Turkey, not hold it as a field
option3: Invalid — adapters can only do 1-to-1 method mapping, never approximate one method with repeated calls to another
option4: Invalid — fly() cannot contain a loop inside an adapter method
correctOptionExplanation: An adapter method's body can contain whatever logic is needed to produce equivalent behavior — including loops or approximations.

questionText: If Duck had a third method, swim(), but Turkey has no swimming-related method at all, what are TurkeyAdapter's realistic options for implementing swim()?
option1: TurkeyAdapter automatically inherits a default swim() from Object
option2: Provide a reasonable best-effort implementation (e.g. print something plausible, or no-op), since implements Duck forces every method to have SOME body — there's no way to partially implement an interface in Java
option3: Delete swim() from the Duck interface so TurkeyAdapter doesn't need to worry about it
option4: Leave swim() unimplemented; Java allows interface methods to be skipped if the underlying class doesn't support them
correctOptionExplanation: Implementing an interface is all-or-nothing in Java (barring default methods) — every abstract method needs a body, even if it's a best-effort stand-in.

questionText: A legacy OldLogger class only has void writeLog(String msg). Your app's newer code depends on an ILogger interface with void info(String msg), void error(String msg), and void debug(String msg). What's the most faithful adapter design, given OldLogger has no concept of log levels?
option1: OldLoggerAdapter cannot be built since OldLogger doesn't natively support log levels
option2: OldLoggerAdapter should throw UnsupportedOperationException for error() and debug() since OldLogger has no equivalent
option3: OldLoggerAdapter implements ILogger, wrapping an OldLogger; each of info()/error()/debug() calls oldLogger.writeLog() with the level prefixed into the message string (e.g. "[ERROR] " + msg), since that's the closest equivalent behavior the legacy class can support
option4: ILogger should be redesigned to only have writeLog(), matching OldLogger exactly
correctOptionExplanation: When the underlying class lacks a concept the target interface expects, the adapter approximates it as closely as it reasonably can rather than failing outright.

questionText: java.util.Collections.enumeration(Collection c) in the real JDK returns an Enumeration wrapping a modern Iterator internally — bridging the old Enumeration API to modern Collection-based code. What role does this JDK method play in Adapter-pattern terms?
option1: It's an example of the Observer pattern, since Enumeration "observes" the collection
option2: It's unrelated to Adapter since it's a built-in JDK method rather than a custom class
option3: It's an example of Singleton, since Collections is a utility class
option4: It's effectively an adapter factory — it returns an object that satisfies the older Enumeration interface while internally delegating to an Iterator, letting legacy code that expects Enumeration work with modern collections
correctOptionExplanation: This is a real, shipped example of Adapter inside the standard library itself — bridging an old API shape to a newer one.

questionText: A checkout system calls IInventoryService.reserveStock(String sku, int qty). You're integrating a newly acquired warehouse partner's SDK, which only exposes WarehouseClient.holdItems(Map<String, Integer> items) (bulk-only, no single-item method). Can a valid adapter still be written for the single-item reserveStock() method?
option1: Yes — WarehouseAdapter.reserveStock(sku, qty) can internally build a single-entry Map<String, Integer> containing just that sku/qty pair and pass it to holdItems(), satisfying the target interface even though the underlying method is bulk-oriented
option2: Yes, but only if WarehouseClient is modified to add a single-item method first
option3: No — an adapter can only be written if the underlying method's parameter count exactly matches the target interface's method
option4: No — adapting a single-item call to a bulk-only method is impossible in Java
correctOptionExplanation: An adapter can call a bulk method with a single-entry collection to simulate a single-item call — no requirement that signatures line up structurally.

questionText: A reporting tool expects data via IReportSource.getRows() returning List<Map<String, String>>. A partner analytics library only exposes AnalyticsClient.fetchXml() returning a raw XML string. Where should the XML-parsing logic live, and why?
option1: Inside AnalyticsClient, requiring you to modify the third-party library's source
option2: Inside the adapter's getRows() implementation — parsing the XML into the expected List<Map<String, String>> shape is exactly the kind of format-translation work an adapter exists to do
option3: It doesn't matter — parsing can happen anywhere in the codebase with identical design quality
option4: Inside IReportSource itself, since all implementers should share parsing logic
correctOptionExplanation: Format translation belongs inside the adapter, keeping the target interface and the rest of the app free of any knowledge of XML.

questionText: If WarehouseAdapter needs to hold a reference to WarehouseClient passed in via its constructor, and WarehouseClient itself has no default no-arg constructor, does this break the adapter pattern?
option1: Yes — every class wrapped by an adapter must have a no-arg constructor by definition
option2: Yes — this would force WarehouseAdapter to extend WarehouseClient instead
option3: No — the adapter just needs to accept whatever's required to construct a working WarehouseClient instance (or receive an already-constructed one) via its own constructor; nothing about Adapter requires the wrapped object to have a no-arg constructor
option4: No, but only if WarehouseClient is later refactored to add a no-arg constructor
correctOptionExplanation: An adapter's constructor can accept an already-built object, or whatever parameters are needed to build one — no constructor shape is mandated.

questionText: Compare Adapter to Decorator, which you've already built with FeeDecorator/RewardDecorator wrapping IPayment. Both wrap an object and implement an interface. What's the actual difference in intent between the two?
option1: Adapter can only wrap one object; Decorator can wrap unlimited objects
option2: There's no real difference — Adapter and Decorator are the same pattern with different class names
option3: Decorator requires an abstract base class; Adapter is not allowed to use one
option4: Adapter exists to make an incompatible interface usable as-is (translating one interface's shape into another, same underlying behavior) — Decorator exists to add new behavior on top of an object that's already compatible with the target interface
correctOptionExplanation: Adapter bridges an incompatible shape into a compatible one; Decorator adds behavior to something already compatible — different problems, similar wrapping structure.

questionText: A NotificationSender interface has void send(String message). You wrap a third-party SMS gateway, TwilioClient.sendSms(String to, String body), inside TwilioAdapter implements NotificationSender. If send(String message) doesn't include a recipient number at all, what real design problem does this expose?
option1: The target interface's method signature is missing information (to) that the underlying SDK actually requires — the adapter can't invent a phone number, so either NotificationSender.send() needs a to parameter, or the adapter needs some other way (e.g. a field set at construction) to know the recipient
option2: The adapter should silently ignore the recipient and just log the message instead
option3: This is not a problem — TwilioClient.sendSms() will use a default recipient automatically
option4: TwilioAdapter should extend TwilioClient to inherit its recipient-handling logic automatically
correctOptionExplanation: Adapter can't manufacture missing information — if the target interface's signature is genuinely too thin, the interface itself needs revisiting.

questionText: A junior dev says: "Why not skip the adapter entirely and just call stripeClient.charge() directly everywhere our code needs to take a payment?" What's the concrete cost of that shortcut?
option1: There's no real cost — calling stripeClient.charge() directly everywhere is equally maintainable
option2: Every call site across the codebase becomes directly coupled to Stripe's specific method names, parameter units (cents vs dollars), and object types — switching payment providers later, or supporting a second provider alongside Stripe, would require editing every one of those call sites instead of just swapping which adapter gets injected
option3: This would only be a problem if the app had more than 100 call sites
option4: stripeClient.charge() cannot be called from outside StripeAdapter in Java, so this isn't actually possible
correctOptionExplanation: Bypassing the adapter reintroduces exactly the tight coupling to a specific vendor's API that the adapter exists to eliminate.

questionText: A DataExporter interface expects byte[] export(). A legacy library gives you LegacyExporter.writeToStream(OutputStream out) (writes to a stream instead of returning bytes directly). How would an adapter bridge this without modifying LegacyExporter?
option1: It's impossible to adapt a stream-based method into a return-value-based method in Java
option2: DataExporter must be redesigned to also use OutputStream so no translation is needed
option3: LegacyExporterAdapter.export() can create an in-memory ByteArrayOutputStream, pass it into legacyExporter.writeToStream(stream), then call stream.toByteArray() and return that — translating a stream-writing style API into a return-value style API
option4: The adapter should call legacyExporter.writeToStream(null) and return an empty array
correctOptionExplanation: Using an in-memory stream to capture the legacy method's output and convert it into the expected return type is a common, valid adapter technique.

questionText: Every adapter you've seen so far — MediaAdapter, StripeAdapter, TurkeyAdapter — HOLDS the incompatible class as a field and delegates to it (composition). Suppose instead someone wrote StripeAdapter extends StripeClient implements PaymentGateway — inheriting from StripeClient directly instead of holding it as a field. In Java specifically, why does this second approach quickly run into trouble if StripeAdapter also needs to inherit from some other class for unrelated reasons?
option1: Extending StripeClient is actually faster at runtime, so this is purely a performance tradeoff with no functional downside
option2: Java forbids extending any class from a third-party library under all circumstances
option3: Holding StripeClient as a field only works if StripeClient is marked final; otherwise extending it is required
option4: Java only allows a class to extend one other class at a time, so if StripeAdapter ever needed to extend something else too, inheriting from StripeClient would block that — holding StripeClient as a field instead avoids this limit entirely, no matter how many classes need bridging
correctOptionExplanation: Composition sidesteps Java's single-inheritance limit — this is the practical reason nearly every real Java adapter wraps rather than extends.

questionText: A ride-hailing app's MapProvider interface has Route getRoute(double startLat, double startLng, double endLat, double endLng). You switch from an in-house mapping service to Google Maps' SDK, which exposes GoogleDirectionsClient.getDirections(LatLng origin, LatLng destination) returning a GoogleRoute object with a different structure than your app's own Route class. What does the adapter need to handle on both ends of the call?
option1: It needs to translate the incoming primitive coordinates into LatLng objects before calling the SDK, and translate the returned GoogleRoute back into your app's own Route type before returning — adapting both the request shape and the response shape
option2: Only the outgoing call needs translation; return types never need adapting
option3: Only the return type needs translation; parameters are always compatible automatically
option4: No translation is needed as long as both classes are named similarly
correctOptionExplanation: A full round-trip adapter often has to translate both directions — what goes in, and what comes back — not just one side of the call.

questionText: If Route and GoogleRoute happen to have completely different field names and structures (e.g. Route.legs vs GoogleRoute.steps), does that make this scenario impossible to adapt cleanly?
option1: Yes — this would require modifying GoogleRoute's source code directly, which you can't do
option2: No — the adapter's job is precisely to do this kind of structural translation; it just means the mapping logic inside the adapter (converting GoogleRoute fields into a new Route object) is more involved, not that it's impossible
option3: Yes — Adapter pattern only works when both classes share identical field names
option4: No, but only if Route and GoogleRoute are converted to use the same package name
correctOptionExplanation: Structural mismatches just mean more translation code inside the adapter — they don't disqualify the approach.

questionText: A photo-editing app has ImageFilter interface with Image apply(Image input). A popular third-party filter library instead exposes static-style utility calls like SepiaUtil.convertToSepia(byte[] rawPixels, int width, int height) and returns byte[]. What additional responsibility does the adapter take on here, beyond simple delegation?
option1: It must make Image extend byte[], which Java supports for arrays
option2: None — it can call SepiaUtil.convertToSepia() directly with the Image object as-is
option3: It must extract raw pixel data (and width/height) out of the app's own Image object before calling the utility method, and reconstruct a new Image object from the returned byte[] afterward — real data marshaling in both directions
option4: It must rewrite SepiaUtil to accept Image objects directly
correctOptionExplanation: When the underlying API works in a totally different data representation, the adapter's job expands to full marshaling, not just a renamed call.

questionText: A music app supports playlists via IPlaylistSource.getTracks() returning List<Track>. You integrate a podcast platform's SDK, PodcastClient.fetchEpisodes(), returning List<Episode> (a totally different class with different fields — Episode has hostName and durationSeconds, Track has artistName and durationMs). Is this a legitimate use case for Adapter?
option1: This requires the Observer pattern instead, since episodes need to notify tracks
option2: This requires the Singleton pattern, since only one podcast client should exist
option3: This is impossible without modifying either Episode or Track's source code
option4: Legitimate Adapter use case — the adapter's getTracks() implementation converts each Episode into a new Track object, mapping hostName to artistName and durationSeconds times 1000 to durationMs, so callers of IPlaylistSource never see Episode at all
correctOptionExplanation: Converting one domain object into another, field by field, inside the adapter's overridden method is a very common and valid adapter shape.

questionText: A test wants to verify that TwilioAdapter.send("hello") actually calls twilioClient.sendSms(...) with the right arguments, without sending a real SMS. What does wrapping TwilioClient via composition (rather than static calls scattered everywhere) make easier here?
option1: You can construct TwilioAdapter with a test double / fake TwilioClient injected via the constructor, and assert on what the fake recorded — the same testability benefit you already saw with ISubscriber test doubles in the Observer pattern
option2: Testing is equally hard either way, since TwilioClient.sendSms() always sends a real SMS regardless of how it's called
option3: You'd need to modify TwilioClient's source code to make it testable
option4: Adapter classes cannot be unit tested by definition, only integration tested
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor-injected dependencies are swappable with fakes/mocks for testing — the same benefit seen throughout the course whenever composition is used over hardcoded references.

questionText: A retail app's ITaxCalculator interface has double calculateTax(double amount, String stateCode). A government tax API SDK instead requires constructing a whole TaxRequest object with a dozen fields (most irrelevant to your use case) and returns a TaxResponse object. What's a reasonable adapter design here?
option1: Every caller of ITaxCalculator should construct their own TaxRequest before calling calculateTax()
option2: GovTaxAdapter implements ITaxCalculator builds a TaxRequest, filling in the fields it actually has data for and using sensible defaults/placeholders for the rest, calls the gov API, and extracts just the tax amount from TaxResponse — the adapter absorbs the complexity of the unfamiliar API entirely
option3: ITaxCalculator.calculateTax() should be changed to accept a full TaxRequest object so no translation work is needed
option4: This scenario cannot be adapted since TaxRequest has more fields than calculateTax()'s parameters
correctOptionExplanation: The adapter absorbing an unfamiliar, heavyweight external API's complexity — so the rest of the app stays simple — is exactly what it's for.

questionText: If two completely different tax APIs (say, a US gov API and a EU VAT API) both need to be adaptable to the same ITaxCalculator interface, how many adapter classes do you need, and does ITaxCalculator itself need to change to support the second one?
option1: ITaxCalculator needs a new method added for every additional API being adapted
option2: Only one adapter is allowed to exist per target interface at any time
option3: Two separate adapter classes (e.g. GovTaxAdapter, VatTaxAdapter), each implementing ITaxCalculator independently — the interface itself needs zero changes, since any number of adapters can implement the same target interface
option4: One adapter class with an if-else branching on which API to call internally
correctOptionExplanation: Any number of independent adapters can implement the same target interface, each hiding a different underlying vendor, with zero changes to the interface or its other implementers.

questionText: A finance app has ICurrencyConverter.convert(double amount, String fromCurrency, String toCurrency). An external exchange-rate API instead only provides ExchangeRateClient.getRate(String pair) returning a double rate for pairs formatted like "USD_EUR". What must the adapter do to bridge these?
option1: ICurrencyConverter should be redesigned to accept a pre-formatted pair string like "USD_EUR" directly
option2: The adapter should just return whatever getRate() returns unmodified, since convert() and getRate() mean the same thing
option3: This cannot be adapted since getRate() doesn't take an amount parameter
option4: RateApiAdapter.convert(amount, from, to) constructs the pair string (e.g. from + "_" + to), calls exchangeRateClient.getRate(pair), and returns amount times rate — handling both the string-formatting translation and the actual multiplication that ICurrencyConverter's contract implies
correctOptionExplanation: The adapter reconciles both a formatting mismatch (pair string construction) and a semantic gap (rate vs converted amount) in one method body.

questionText: A smart-home app has ISmartDevice.turnOn()/turnOff(). You integrate three different vendors' bulbs — one SDK uses setPower(true/false), another uses activate()/deactivate(), a third uses on()/off(). After writing three separate adapters (VendorAAdapter, VendorBAdapter, VendorCAdapter), what does the rest of your smart-home app's code look like when controlling any bulb, regardless of vendor?
option1: Identical — the rest of the app only ever calls device.turnOn()/device.turnOff() on the ISmartDevice interface, completely unaware of which vendor SDK or method names are underneath any given adapter instance
option2: Each vendor's bulbs require entirely separate control code paths in the app
option3: The app still needs an if(vendor.equals("A")) check before calling any device method
option4: The app must know which adapter class is in use to call the correct vendor-specific method name
correctOptionExplanation: This is the ultimate payoff of Adapter: the rest of the app is fully decoupled from vendor-specific method names, no matter how many vendors exist.

questionText: Tie it together: across weather sensors, payment gateways, shipping vendors, tax APIs, and smart bulbs, every single adapter example above followed the identical shape — implements TargetInterface, holds the incompatible object via composition, translates data/calls inside the overridden method(s). What's the one-sentence summary of what Adapter actually is, as distinct from just "wrapping a class"?
option1: Adapter specifically requires the wrapped class and the target interface to have at least one identical method name
option2: Adapter is specifically about making an object usable through an interface it wasn't originally built to satisfy, by translating calls/data between the two shapes — not every class that "wraps" another object is doing this (e.g. Decorator wraps too, but to add behavior to an already-compatible interface, not to translate an incompatible one)
option3: Adapter means any class that has a field referencing another object, regardless of interfaces involved
option4: Adapter is only valid when integrating third-party SDKs, never for two classes within the same codebase
correctOptionExplanation: The defining trait of Adapter is bridging an incompatible interface into a compatible one — the distinguishing detail from other wrapping patterns like Decorator.
